questions.prompt: Complete: "Our headmaster ___ going to organise an excursion next month."
questions.explanation: "Our headmaster" is one person, like he, so be going to takes is: he is going to organise an excursion. "are" is for we / you / they, "am" only for I, and "be" is not a present form.

questions.prompt: Complete the promise: "I ___ never do it again, I promise."
questions.explanation: A promise about the future uses will + bare infinitive: I will never do it again. "won't" + never makes a double negative, which English refuses; "am" + do is not a verb form; "going to" alone drops "am".

won't is the short form of will not, the negative of the future tense: it won't be expensive = it will not be expensive. It has nothing to do with want, and "were not" / "did not" are past forms (weren't, didn't).

options.text: Do you thinking of studying abroad?
Are you thinking to study abroad?
Are you thinking of to study abroad?
Are you thinking of studying abroad?

questions.explanation: In a question with be thinking of, only are moves before the subject, and the verb after of keeps -ing: Are you thinking of studying abroad? "Do you thinking" uses do with an -ing form; "thinking to study" borrows the to of intend; "of to study" mixes the two structures.

questions.prompt: Find the error: "Will she comes to the party tomorrow?"
questions.explanation: The error is "comes": after will the verb is a bare infinitive, even with she — Will she come to the party tomorrow? "Will" correctly opens the question, and "to the party" and "tomorrow" are correct.

questions.prompt: Complete the answer: "What do you intend to do after the Baccalaureate?" — "I ___ medicine."
questions.explanation: intend to + base verb: I intend to study medicine. "intend to studying" puts -ing after to; "am intend" adds be to an ordinary verb in the present; "intending to study" has no subject verb at all.
